entries.title: In only their second season, Valkyries win WNBA Finals
entries.summary: <p>SAN FRANCISCO — Gabby Williams scored her team's final 11 points of the third quarter and dazzled through the fourth on the way to 30 points, and the Golden State Valkyries captured a championship in just their second season by beating the Atlanta Dream 68-63 in a sensational first WNBA Finals Game 7 on Saturday night.</p><p>Jordin Canada scored 18 points, Allisha Gray 16 and Angel Reese had eight points and 12 rebounds for the Dream, denied another championship in the franchise's fourth try.</p><p>Gray made two free throws with 11 seconds left then Atlanta forced a jump ball — Gray against Williams — and Veronica Burton corralled it and converted two free throws with 5.1 seconds to go.</p><p>“I'm just so blessed, this is insane!” said Burton, cut by Dallas two years ago.</p><p>Rhyne Howard's layup tied it at 57 with 2:41 left only for Williams to answer once more with a clutch 3-pointer. She converted two free throws with 1:40 remaining, then Kiah Stokes scored a late basket. Stokes pulled down 13 rebounds and blocked two more shots to cap her spectacular postseason.</p><p>Williams left Seattle with a great feeling about joining Golden State and its close-knit culture, returning to the Bay Area where she played youth basketball to build something special with the Valkyries — and she’s now done that. Fans chanted “Gabby! Gabby!” throughout the fourth quarter.</p><p>“All it took was good people,” she said. “All we heard last year was we don’t have no stars. We don’t have no talent. Yeah right! We got good people. We got good people. We got winners. We got people who are ready to put their bodies on the floor to win a game.”</p><p>When the final buzzer sounded, the violet-clad sellout crowd at Chase Center went into a frenzy as players sprinted onto the floor to hug and celebrate as confetti fell from the rafters.</p><p>“Ballhalla” had become “Boohalla” for this far-but-haunted Halloween night in the raucous arena. Now, with a women's championship to its name right alongside the one earned by the Golden State Warriors in 2022.</p><p>“We gotta build a bigger trophy case,” co-owner Peter Guber said.</p><p>The team that led at halftime in the first six matchups had won every game so far, and the Dream were ahead 30-24 at the break. Atlanta also had been 16-0 this season when Reese made at least one 3. The Dream's DeWanna Bonner became the first player in WNBA history to reach 600 career postseason defensive rebounds.</p><p>Valkyries coach Natalie Nakase changed her starting lineup in a move that paid huge dividends after Golden State fell behind 2-1, inserting Kaila Charles and Tiffany Hayes and bringing Kayla Thornton and Cecilia Zandalasini off the bench.</p><p>The 37-year-old Hayes, who came out of retirement two years ago and spent 10 seasons with the Dream, scored 11 points in the winner-take-all Game 7 and brought energy all series that made Nakase want to win for the veteran guard as much as anybody.</p><p>Valkyries owner Joe Lacob guaranteed a championship within the first five years for this franchise three years ago when the Bay Area was granted an expansion team, and in improbable, joyful fashion, his team accomplished it in Year 2. That after becoming the first expansion organization to reach the playoffs in its inaugural year in 2025.</p><p>During the victory ceremony, Lacob shouted out the team and its leaders, while Nakase, general manager Ohemma Nyanin and President Jess Smith hugged. And Lacob thanked the fans who have sold out Chase Center for every game since Day 1.</p><p>“Ballhalla!” Lacob hollered.</p>

entries.title: Chicago man charged with 14 felonies after Evanston police seize drugs, firearms
entries.summary: <p>A Chicago man is facing 14 felony charges after Evanston police seized suspected drugs, four firearms and several suspected homemade incendiary devices during a search of his home Friday afternoon.</p><p>Ernest W. Pentek, 48, was arrested just after 2 p.m. Friday as officers carried out a search warrant at his residence in the 6900 block of North Ashland Avenue, according to an Evanston Police Department press release.</p><p>The department’s Special Operations Group investigated information that Pentek was allegedly distributing narcotics in Evanston and Chicago and possessed firearms and potentially dangerous incendiary devices, police said.</p><p>Officers recovered more than 500 grams of suspected methamphetamine, 7.1 grams of heroin, 11 grams of Xanax, 4 grams of crack cocaine, 39 MDMA pills and about 2.6 pounds of cannabis, police said.</p><p>Officers also recovered a substance believed to be gamma-hydroxybutyrate, or GHB, an airsoft rifle, ballistic protective equipment and $1,185, police said.</p><p>Pentek was charged with four counts of unlawful possession of a firearm by a felon and one count of aggravated unlawful possession of a weapon involving a shotgun with a barrel shorter than 18 inches, police said.</p><p>He also faces one count each of possession of methamphetamine with intent to deliver, possession of methamphetamine, possession of a controlled substance with intent to deliver, possession of cannabis with intent to deliver and possession of cannabis, along with four counts of possession of a controlled substance, according to police.</p><p>Evanston police’s Special Response Team and the Cook County Bomb Squad assisted in the search. Chicago police also assisted in the operation, Evanston police said.</p><p>Pentek was scheduled for an initial court appearance Saturday at the George N. Leighton Criminal Court Building, according to the release.</p>

entries.title: Noah Taylor, Sean Rice lead resurgent St. Laurence past Plainfield South in 7A playoffs
entries.summary: <p>No one would have blamed St. Laurence linebacker Sean Rice if he had called it a year when he suffered maybe the strangest injury of the football season.</p><p>He is a three-star prospect committed to Illinois, and the injury-riddled Vikings were 1-5.</p><p>But Rice is back, and so is St. Laurence.</p><p>Rice led a strong defensive effort, and Noah Taylor threw two touchdown passes as the Vikings beat host Plainfield South 28-13 in the first round of the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/2026/10/17/ihsa-state-football-playoff-pairings-class7a-illinois-2026" target="_blank" >Class 7A</a> playoffs Saturday.</p><p>‘‘Oh, my gosh, it’s amazing,’’ Rice said of playing again. ‘‘When I got hurt, it was a scary moment because I had some people telling me I wasn’t going to play again in my high school career. I had people telling me, ‘No, it’s not worth it to play another snap in high school football.’ But this team means the world to me, and getting back on the field is all that mattered.’’</p><p>The injury? He hurt an ankle running through a banner before a game.</p><p>‘‘The cheer girls told me after the game that they did the Velcro too tight, so it felt like running into a wall,’’ Rice said. ‘‘But things happen, so you’ve just got to work through it.’’</p><p>St. Laurence (5-6) held the Cougars (8-2) scoreless for the last 2½ quarters, getting an interception from Tony Cruz and a red-zone stop that ended with a missed field goal.</p><p>‘‘I think we had a big shift on our team after Week 6,’’ Rice said. ‘‘We realized that we have dudes on this team. We have leaders. We have guys that can step up and make big plays in big moments. So I think that just shows that we’re the grittiest team that you can find.’’</p><p>Taylor, a junior, is one of those who stepped up. He was 16-for-28 for 214 yards with touchdowns of 48 yards to Jackson Kavois and 20 yards to Dakarai Simmons. He also ran 13 times for 100 yards, and the Vikings got touchdown runs from Keynan Morgan and Dave Campbell.</p><p>‘‘You knew he was a really good runner all year,’’ St. Laurence coach Pat Swanson said of Taylor. ‘‘He does some really special things in that department, makes us really good there. But to see his progression as a passer throughout the year, it’s special to see the light bulb turn on a little bit for some guys and to see some of our receivers on the outside help him out and find ways to get open.’’</p><p>‘‘Honestly, I’ve been counted out in the pass game by a lot of people,’’ Taylor said. ‘‘Everybody tells me I’m a run-first quarterback, like I shouldn’t be out there playing quarterback. But I’ve played quarterback all my life, and I knew that I had it in me.’’</p><p>Plainfield South sophomore Armani Ford was 19-for-36 for 206 yards with two touchdowns, including a 70-yarder to Liem Sesta, and one interception. The Cougars won the Southwest Prairie East and had their best record in 16 years.</p><p>‘‘I’m going to miss the ones who are leaving,’’ Plainfield South coach Rob Szudarski said. ‘‘But they laid the standards and the foundation for us. And the others understand what it’s going to take now to get to this level and to do this year after year.</p><p>‘‘We want to be a perennial playoff team. We don’t want to be one year in and one year out.’’</p>

entries.title: 1 killed, two wounded in North Lawndale shooting
entries.summary: <p>A 29-year-old man was killed and two other people wounded in a shooting Saturday afternoon in North Lawndale, Chicago police said.</p><p>At 5:18 p.m., men ages 23 and 29, and a 35-year-old woman were standing on a sidewalk in the 3400 block of West Ogden Avenue when a vehicle pulled up to them, police said.</p><p>Two unidentified people then got out of the car and fired shots at all three victims before fleeing westbound on Ogden Avenue, according to police.</p><p>The 29-year-old man was shot in the chest and taken to Stroger Hospital, where he later died, police said. The 23-year-old was shot in the stomach and taken to Mount Sinai Hospital in critical condition, police said.</p><p>The woman — shot in the left leg — was transported to the same hospital in good condition, police said.</p><p>Area 4 detectives are investigating, police said.</p>

entries.title: What to consider if a company that made AI-related job cuts wants you back
entries.summary: <p>Companies around the world are increasingly citing artificial intelligence when slashing jobs, fueling anxiety that a lot more workers may lose their livelihoods to machines.</p><p>Microsoft, Barclays Bank and supermarket chain Kroger are among the latest entries on a growing list of companies that have announced AI-related workforce reductions this year, including the elimination of jobs deemed redundant or shed to free up money for investing in the technology.</p><p>But the job cuts of the AI era, which are affecting tens of thousands of people, occasionally have an epilogue. Some companies, after discovering that AI models, applications and agents don't perform as well as expected, end up rehiring laid-off workers to fill eliminated positions.</p><p>It's unclear how common such reversals are, but they are happening often enough to acquire a nickname: the “AI boomerang."</p><p>“Two years ago, we said, ‘Would this happen?’ and now we’re saying, ‘Yes, it is happening in real time,’” said Lucy Beaumont, global senior vice president at SHL, a U.K.-based technology company that develops employment-related tests and tools.</p><p>Hiring managers in fields including finance, marketing, law and health reported earlier this year that their companies had eliminated positions primarily because of AI or automation, only to hire again for the same or similar roles, according to recruitment and staffing firm Robert Half.</p><p>The most frequently cited reasons for restoring dropped jobs included the technology needing more human oversight than anticipated and its inability to replicate institutional knowledge, the firm said.</p><p>“When you need critical thinking, collaboration, creativity, institutional knowledge, those are things that AI just can’t replicate,” Bill Driscoll, senior district president at Robert Half, said. “And I think that’s where companies are starting to realize, ‘Wow, we really do need people to do these jobs.’”</p><p>Klarna, the Swedish provider of buy now, pay later services, began recruiting human customer service representatives again last year. CEO Sebastian Siemiatkowski acknowledged in an interview with Bloomberg News that the company’s reliance on an AI chatbot to cut costs had gone too far.</p><p>In June, Ford said it had hired or promoted 350 veteran engineers after AI tools the automaker deployed to do quality control work didn't perform at the expected level.</p><p>However, companies don’t always broadcast their U-turns on shifting resources or responsibilities from employees to AI systems, Beaumont said.</p><p>“Maybe their shareholders love that they did this right-sizing motion ... and then they have to turn around and quietly, with their tail between their legs, admit that they weren’t ready for that or they shouldn’t have done that,” she said.</p><p>When companies use AI to perform tasks previously done by people, they often miss the invisible work employees do beyond their formal job descriptions, said Betsy Summers, principal analyst on the Future of Work team at market research and advisory firm Forrester.</p><p>That might include sensing emotions and moods, holding impromptu meetings and putting in extra effort when feeling inspired or otherwise motivated, Summers said.</p><p>Another factor that complicates assigning more work to AI-powered tools is that company procedures for tasks such as data processing and bookkeeping are not always well documented, experts said.</p><p>“Organizations are not spending enough time doing the up-front work to really truly understand workflows and where humans add value in the process,” said Brooks Holtom, professor of management at Georgetown University’s McDonough School of Business.</p><p>In roles such as customer service, AI agents and chatbots frequently need to refer questions and complaints to a worker who can recognize emotions, assess the severity or complexity of a problem and respond creatively within established policies, Holtom said.</p><p>Many people are understandably reluctant to return to a company that laid them off as part of a reorganization around artificial intelligence, according to Beaumont.</p><p>Workers offered their old jobs back are asking for more money and to know how AI might impact future staffing, Beaumont said. Requesting additional training and a clear explanation of your opportunities for advancement could be part of the discussion, she said.</p><p>Communicate ways you would contribute value as a returning employee, outlining a new job description “that leverages the technology but also your expertise,” Holtom said. You could end up in a higher-ranking position that pays more than the one you left, he said.</p><p>Before accepting an offer, seek a commitment such as a one-year renewable contract that includes a buyout clause if the job is terminated in less than a year, Holtom suggested.</p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Neighbors tire of maintaining derelict property
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> How much should a neighborhood do to keep up a vacant house? About 15 years ago, a couple in their 50s moved into the end of my cul-de-sac. Their two children were out of college; the son lived elsewhere, and the daughter lived with them.</p><p>Almost two years ago, the dad died suddenly. The mom moved out of state with relatives. The house has been vacant ever since. There are five cars on the property: one in the side yard, two in the driveway and two parked in the street in front. (There is limited parking in the cul-de-sac.) We have asked the children to sell or move the cars, but nothing has been done. The taillights have been broken, and in one car a window is down, and kids can get into it. When can we ask the police to declare the cars abandoned and tow them?</p><p>The son comes by about once a month to get the mail. Bill collectors come by and ask how to get in touch with the owners. Even the utilities aren't paid. When I called the daughter about all this, she suggested I give out her brother's phone number. Is it our responsibility to help creditors and utilities get in touch with the owners' children?</p><p>Several of us regularly pick up litter that blows into the yard. I raked up leaves in the fall. I watered the roses in summer. I am older than the owner and don't want to look after two yards. Do you have any suggestions? — <i>NETTLED NEIGHBOR</i></p><p><b>DEAR NEIGHBOR:</b> Sympathy for the bereaved is all well and good, but after two years of this, enough is enough. You've gone above and beyond as a generous neighbor, and it's time to recognize that your efforts have not been appreciated. Do not set foot on that property again to do free yard work.</p><p>The abandoned cars are a safety concern and should be reported to the police immediately. As for the creditors, by all means provide them with the son's contact information. It's not your responsibility, but they'll have no reason to bother you after that. For all the other unsightly concerns that have accumulated, make a detailed list and report everything to the city. I'm willing to bet the place gets cleaned up (or sold) in a hurry once municipal fines have been assessed.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I have had a best friend, "Carolyn," since seventh grade. Her husband died more than 10 years ago, and every year a graduating senior receives a small scholarship in his memory.</p><p>This year, my granddaughter graduated, which Carolyn surely knows, yet Carolyn's family awarded the scholarship to another senior. I am so hurt by this I don't know how to handle it. Any ideas? — <i>SLIGHTED IN PENNSYLVANIA</i></p><p><b>DEAR SLIGHTED:</b> Has it not occurred to you that the student who was awarded the small scholarship may have needed it more than your granddaughter? Your friendship with Carolyn should not be a factor in who received the award. Handle your disappointment by recognizing that you were wrong to assume your granddaughter would be guaranteed anything.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.</i></p>

entries.title: Cubs' Mike Montgomery had the all-time moment in 2016. After that? Baseball wasn't easy
entries.summary: <p>Mike Montgomery got the call. Then he got the ground ball.</p><p>A man could live 1,000 baseball lives and never come through in a bigger moment than two outs in the 10th inning of Game 7 of the 2016 World Series in Cleveland.</p><p>Throughout Cubdom, Montgomery’s one-out save — the first of his professional career — will live forever. Ten years since Nov. 2, 2016, the 37-year-old still can close his eyes and feel the rush of it.</p><p>“The highest high imaginable,” he says.</p><p>How many pitchers can say they got a final out that endures as toweringly as that one? But baseball isn’t a storybook, and Montgomery had to fight with all his might for every inch of success in the game after the night to end all nights. A former Royals first-round pick who threw back-to-back shutouts in his first month in the majors with the Mariners in 2015, Montgomery still believed after being traded to the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" target="_blank" >Cubs</a> in July of 2016 that he could become “one of the best players ever in the game.” Needless to say, that didn’t happen.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="113" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/HOp8w2PgHlM?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Cubs win World Series with Game 7 win"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>Instead, a lefty whom Kyle Hendricks predicted the following spring would become the Cubs’ next pitching star lasted another two-plus seasons on the North Side — never truly locking down a rotation spot — and was dealt in 2019 back to the Royals, with whom he fizzled out. From there, it was an odyssey: Montgomery was released in spring training by the Mets, bombed out in the minors with the Yankees, had an unsuccessful stint in Korea, gave it another go with the Mets in Triple-A but got shelled, signed with a Mexican League team but was soon released, pitched forgettably in the Dodgers’ system and in 2024 — making less than $3,000 a month in one last gasp — turned out to be just another arm for the Long Island Ducks of the independent Atlantic League.</p><p>It was over.</p><p>No more storybook moments. No more dream.</p><p>Fortunately, no regrets the size of which keep a man up at night.</p><p>“I’ve been in the highest of highs and then been in Mexico sitting there sick from the water, thinking, ‘What am I doing? I’ve got a two-year-old and a daughter about to be born.’ In Long Island, here I am a World Series champ with six years in the big leagues. I was throwing 90, 92, thought my stuff was good enough, but nobody called. …</p><p>“But I’ve talked with some close friends and my wife about this: What if I would’ve had a 12-year career and made hundreds of millions but never won anything? To be a part of one of the best moments in baseball history, I don’t think there’s enough money for that. I wouldn’t trade it for anything. It’s not like we’re broke. I could’ve had a better career, made more, but I had the kind of pinnacle moment that I can take with me forever.”</p><p>Since May, Montgomery, who lives in Scottsdale, Arizona, with his family, has been the rehab pitching coach for the Mariners, a job he’s enjoying. Son Max and daughter Zoe are growing. Life is good. Any regrets are small enough.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-e00000" entries.summary: <p>Several of the state’s best teams welcomed back star players from injury this week, but the biggest injury news is the return of Oswego running back Ammar Banire.</p><p>Banire was the breakout star of last season’s Class 8A playoffs, leading the Panthers to the state championship game with a quarterfinal win against Maine South and a semifinal <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/2025/11/22/oswego-high-school-football-ihsa-state-lockport" >victory over Lockport</a>.</p><p>Since then, the 6-2, 190-pound junior has received scholarship offers from Oklahoma State and several Big Ten schools. He visited Notre Dame in early October.</p><p>Banire missed Oswego’s last five regular-season games, and his playoff status was completely unknown before the weekend. The Panthers are a solid team and could compete against any of the 8A powers without him, but Banire is a special talent who elevates the team to another level.</p><p>Banire returned in style in the first round against Naperville Central. He scored a 31-yard touchdown on his first touch and finished with seven carries for 118 yards and two touchdowns, all in the first half of the Panthers’ 27-6 win.</p><p>Oswego hosts Naperville North in the second round this weekend.</p><h3>Public League flowers</h3><p>It was a banner weekend for Public League football teams. Lane, Kenwood, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/2026/10/31/eshun-flowers-punt-block-td-sparks-simeon-to-a-6a-playoff-win-over-oak-lawn" >Simeon</a>, King and Morgan Park all advanced to the second round of the playoffs. And they didn’t sneak in. The Public League winners may not have knocked off football powerhouses, but all five victories were against legitimate, established schools: South Elgin, Glenbard East, Oak Lawn, Deerfield and Oak Forest.</p><p>This may not be the end of the road for the Public League. Huntley is a heavy favorite over Lane in 8A, and Simeon is an underdog against Nazareth in 6A. But King will have an outside shot against Cary-Grove in 5A, as will Kenwood against Normal in 7A.</p><p>Morgan Park faces a major challenge against Providence in 5A. The Mustangs are underdogs, but still the most likely team to advance to the quarterfinals.</p><h3>Goode entertains the state</h3><p>And then there is Goode. The little-known Southwest Side school played an <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/10/30/little-known-goode-entertains-the-state-in-88-84-playoff-loss-to-quincy-played-at-two-different-fields" >astounding Class 6A state playoff game</a> against visiting Quincy. The Knights lost 88-84 in a game that started at 3 p.m., lasted four hours, set multiple state records, and had to be moved to Englewood’s stadium when darkness set in. Goode’s field has no lights.</p><p>The combined 172 points is the most ever in a high school game in Illinois, topping the 166 scored when Springfield beat Rock Island 94-72 on October 29, 2021. Quincy quarterback Bryson Little threw a state-record nine touchdown passes and rushed for two TDs.</p><p>“This is why we love high school sports,” IHSA Executive Director Craig Anderson said. “The circumstances weren’t ideal, but everyone involved came together on behalf of students, and the result is something that no one involved with this game is ever going to forget.”</p><h3>Super 25 updates</h3><p>Kankakee and Sandburg fall out of the rankings after losing in the first round of the playoffs. The Eagles were ranked most of the season, and Kankakee has been in the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/super-25-football-rankings/2026/10/25/high-school-football-rankings-chicago-illinois-sun-times-michael-obrien" >Super 25</a> since the preseason.</p><p>Several contenders vied for the two open spots. entries.title: Pivoting from the Day of the Dead to the Day of the Election
entries.summary: <p>Happy Days of the Dead!</p><p>OK, first off, you're not supposed to say "happy," despite all the colorful <i>calaveras de azúcar</i><i>, </i>or sugar skulls, and boisterous street parties. Because the Day of the Dead, unlike Halloween, is not a peripatetic candy festival for kids that has been retrofitted into a costumed beer bash for adults. But a solemn, reflective time of honoring lost loved ones.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-110000" name="module-110000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Opinion bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Opinion</h2></div> </div><p>And second, as mentioned above, it is <i>"</i><i>Day</i> of the Dead," singular, <i>Día de los Muertos</i>. Even though there are at least two days, Nov. 1 and 2, the first to remember lost children, <i>Día de los Angelitos</i>, which is an agony almost too great to consider — heck, it's hard enough when your children survive, grow up on schedule, excel, get married and go off to live in Washington, D.C., where you hardly ever see them.</p><p>And the second, Monday, <i>Día de los Difuntos</i><i>,</i> or "All Souls Day," dedicated to adults. For starters. Some mark four, or even eight days, referring to the "Week of the Dead." </p><p>Complicated, right? You can see why a lot of folks ignore cultures other than their own. Once you start to unpack the actual details, there's a lot to keep track of, and it's easier to neglect something than to be wrong about it.</p><p>Nor is the holiday limited to solemnizing your own family. There is, for instance, a strong political element, usually completely overlooked, lost amid the sugary bread.</p><p>We might, for instance, pause to remember all the children who are gone but not dead, those in ICE custody. They are alive, though children, separated from their parents and plunged alone into a nighmarish, unending confinement in a sprawling police state who might easily wish they were dead. They're not your children; but they're somebody's children, and while this might be hard for you to wrap your head around, those children are loved and missed as much as you love and would miss yours, if some performatively cruel government separated you from them to score points with its howling base. Maybe more.</p><p>We might also consider the departed who aren't blood relatives. Especially with Tuesday being what we could call the <i>Día de la Elección</i> — the Day of the Election — most likely, although at this point, we really can't be certain, can we?</p><p>Picking someone at random, I'd go with Dolores Huerta, the labor leader and civil rights icon who died last week at 96. She was given the front-page treatment she deserved. But a life as long and rich as hers, important aspects were given short shrift. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/obituaries/2026/10/28/dolores-huerta-influential-labor-leader-feminist-and-civil-rights-icon-dies-at-96" target="_blank" >The Sun-Times obituary </a>of Huerta mentions voting exactly once, in passing, certainly nowhere near the treatment given her sharing that she had been sexually abused.</p><p>So let's glance at last year's <a class="Link" href="https://fairelectionscenter.org/media/dolores-huerta-a-life-of-activism-justice-and-voting-rights/" target="_blank" >Fair Elections Center</a> tribute:</p><p>"In the 1950s, Huerta co-founded the Community Service Organization (CSO) to help Latino communities fight discrimination, economic hardships, and voter suppression.</p><p>"Huerta understood that political power was essential for lasting change. She worked tirelessly to ensure that farmworkers and Latinos had access to the ballot box, despite widespread voter suppression.</p><p>"She led voter registration drives, often going door-to-door in rural communities to help people overcome language barriers, intimidation, and unfair literacy tests. She also pushed for the elimination of poll taxes, which disproportionately affected poor and minority voters.</p><p>"During the 1960s and 1970s, she played a crucial role in mobilizing Latino voters, helping to elect leaders who would fight for workers’ rights. She worked closely with Robert F. Kennedy, and in 1968, she stood by his side the night he won the California Democratic primary — just moments before he was assassinated.</p><p>"Huerta also helped advocate for the 1965 Voting Rights Act, which prohibited racial discrimination in voting and empowered more Latino communities to participate in elections."</p><p>You get the point.</p><p>Everything old is new again, and the efforts of the Trump administration to cast doubt on, undermine and control elections are a rush back to a bad place we were once at and will return to again unless vigorously opposed.</p><p>I hear from people who seem to think some moment of liberation is at hand, and to them, I typically deploy a rare sports metaphor: "Don't spike the ball until you're in the end zone."</p><p>Freedom is not free, as the vets like to say, nor is it permanent. Someone is always trying to take it away, and maybe one problem is we didn't really appreciate what we have. What we <i>had.</i> Millions of Americans fought to get us here.</p><p>During the Day of the Dead, the barrier to the other world is supposedly thinner, more porous, and if we listen hard, we can almost hear their voices saying: "Don't squander the treasure we won for you. Make this right."</p>

entries.title: Man killed during argument in Chicago Lawn
entries.summary: <p>A 41-year-old man was fatally shot during an argument early Sunday in the Chicago Lawn neighborhood, according to Chicago police.</p><p>The man was arguing with an unknown person around 2 a.m. in the 6500 block of South Francisco Avenue. The unknown person pulled out a gun and shot the man before fleeing, police said. The man was taken to Holy Cross Hospital where he was pronounced dead.</p><p>Police have not announced any arrests.<br></p>

entries.title: Man dies after crashing car into tree
entries.summary:
A 34-year-old man died after he lost control of his car and crashed into a tree early Sunday in the Morgan Park neighborhood, Chicago police said.

The man was driving a black electric car in the 11300 block of South Western Avenue at around 12:45 a.m. when he crashed. The car immediately caught on fire, according to police. Chicago firefighters extinguished the flames and found the man in the driver's seat.

He was pronounced dead at the scene, police said. No one else was in the car.

entries.title: 15-year-old boy shot in Austin
entries.summary: <p>A 15-year-old boy out with friends was shot early Sunday in the Austin neighborhood, according to Chicago police.</p><p>The boy and his friends were in the 5400 block of West Fulton Street just before 1 a.m. when an unknown male approached the group and started arguing with them, police said. He pulled out a gun and fired. The teen was shot in his thigh and taken to Mount Sinai Hospital in good condition.</p><p>The shooter fled, and police have not announced any arrests. </p>

entries.title: Caleb Williams for MVP? Monday is a prime time to state his case
entries.summary: <p>Whether Caleb Williams gives himself a chance to win NFL MVP or not, it won’t be for lack of exposure.</p><p>If he were in the running for the Heisman Trophy, the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears’</a> prime-time broadcast run between now and Christmas would be a point in his favor. If the quarterback was running for Senate, national television games would be his big end-of-cycle ad buy.</p><p>Monday night’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/10/31/bears-report-te-colston-loveland-good-to-go-vs-seahawks-despite-neck-injury" target="_blank" >game in Seattle</a>, then, figures to chart the course for the next two months of Williams discourse. He’s got the seventh-best odds to win the MVP, at 22-1, despite missing three games due to injury. But he has plenty of prominent opportunities — against some of the NFL’s best teams — to state his case.</p><p>“You have to hold yourself to a certain standard,” Williams said. “And that's what these primetime games are — they're the league seeing us as one of those teams that's the best in football.”</p><p>The Bears improved to 5-2 with a primetime win against the Patriots. They’ll follow their “Monday Night Football” game with a “Sunday Night Football” matchup against the Buccaneers at Soldier Field.On Thanksgiving, he’ll play a standalone game against the Lions. On Dec. 19, the Bears will play a prime-time Saturday night game in Buffalo. Their rivalry game against the Packers at noon Christmas Day will be the only game in its time slot, too. That list doesn’t include any possible flexed-game scenarios, either — if the Bears remain one of the hottest teams in football, they could play even more night games.</p><p>“We want to go out there and prove ourselves each and every week — it doesn't matter if it's primetime or not,” Williams said. “But in that sense of it being primetime, that's what the league wants for us. That's what we want for ourselves.”</p><p>When the Bears traded for four-time Pro Bowl defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons this week — and the Seahawks for eight-time Pro Bowl guard Quenton Nelson — Monday night’s game became, for some, a preview of the NFC championship. It will also be another national referendum on Williams and his chances to be considered among the best players — at any position — in the NFL.</p><p>“This isn't a rival game for us, but it's a big game,” Williams said. “It's on primetime. They're going to be loud. They're the reigning champs, and so I'm excited for it.”</p><p>He has every reason to be. Williams is trending the way the Bears have always dreamed, posting a completion percentage above coach Ben Johnson’s stated goal of 70% and throwing only one interception in four games. He posted a passer rating of 111.2 against the Falcons and 116.7 against the Patriots after returning from a hamstring injury. Johnson thought he could have been better against the Patriots, though — and the quarterback agreed.</p><p>“I love just where he is, mindset-wise, right now,” Johnson said. “No one's more critical of him than himself at this point. And as good as he's done taking care of the football — and certainly the higher completion percentage and all those things — we would come in, and there's a lot more to be had last week.”</p><p>Williams’ performances encouraged general manager Ryan Poles to trade two first-round picks as part of a package for Simmons as part of the Bears’ Super Bowl push.</p><p>“A lot of hope and belief in our quarterback — and the path that he's on,” Poles said.</p><p>It’s been since the Bears’ last Super Bowl appearance, probably, that the Bears were considered such a serious contender to win a championship. The monoliths that stood in front of them last year — the Rams and Seahawks — aren’t running away with the NFC as the season comes close to its halfway point.</p><p>Monday night, then, will be a measuring stick.</p><p>“We've been saying all week long that we're gonna have to coach the best that we've coached all year, we're gonna have to play the best that we've played all year,” Johnson said. “And that doesn't mean we're scared to make mistakes or anything like that, but we got to be on our mess. We can't shoot ourselves in the foot with turnovers or penalties or things of that nature. ….</p><p>“It'll be a great tape to look at, just to assess where we are.”</p><p>And where Williams is. Last week, the Seahawks bullied Patrick Mahomes into the worst game of his illustrious career. The Chiefs scored just three points and didn’t post a pass of at least 20 yards or a run of at least 10. None of that had ever happened with Mahomes under center.</p><p>When Williams walks to the line of scrimmage Monday, the Seahawks will be in a shell with two high safeties. Their coverage, though, will morph depending on what the Bears do immediately after the snap. If the Bears send a running back into the flat quickly, for example, a safety could cover him. If the release is slow, though, the safety would go elsewhere.</p><p>“You may not know what the coverage is at any given time or where the pressure's coming from at any given time,” offensive coordinator Press Taylor said. “And we try to build in this standard operating procedure of how we're going to respond to any of it — and all of it — and make sure we're putting our guys in the best position.”</p><p>Williams needs to know the rules of the defense, then, and play with enough anticipation to attack it. That’s a tough ask.</p><p>Master it, though, and Williams could start stating his MVP case.</p>

entries.title: Which scoring wingers could the Blackhawks target in trade negotiations?
entries.summary: <p>One way the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a> could address their roster's flaws and inject life into their season before it fully slips away is by making a trade.</p><p>The NHL trade market is typically quiet this early in the season, but this is no typical season. The Red Wings' messy Dylan Larkin and Simon Edvinsson situations remain unresolved, and Lightning star Nikita Kucherov just shook the earth with his shocking trade request Friday.</p><p>It wouldn't make sense for the Hawks to pursue Larkin or Kucherov, given their ages — 30 and 33, respectively — and how much it would take to acquire them. Nor would either of them approve a trade to Chicago in all likelihood.</p><p>Nonetheless, Hawks general manager Kyle Davidson could attempt to take advantage of the excitement and instability they're introducing into the market or the domino effects that might occur after one gets dealt.</p><p>It sounds like Davidson is working the phones, at least. NHL reporter Frank Seravalli said Tuesday on Chicago Sports Network that the Hawks are specifically looking for a "shoot-first scoring winger with size."</p><p>The Hawks definitely lack size among their top-nine forwards, and coach Jeff Blashill has been calling for an increased <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/10/24/chicago-blackhawks-shots-on-goal-scoring-chances-connor-bedard-patrick-kane-jeff-blashill-andrew-mangiapane-bowen-byram" >shooting mentality</a>, so that prototype makes sense.</p><p>Based on my guesswork, here are a few players who could be Hawks targets:</p><p>Capitals forward Ivan Miroshnichenko has reportedly requested a trade because he has been healthy-scratched for all but three games this season. The 22-year-old Russian has good size (6-1 and 205 pounds), skates well and was productive in the AHL the last two seasons (76 points in 94 games combined).</p><p>He's in a similar position to Hawks defenseman Kevin Korchinski, who was taken 13 picks before Miroshnichenko in the 2022 first round. Both are in limbo because they're no longer waiver-exempt. Perhaps the Hawks and Capitals could work out a swap? Then again, the Capitals' strong roster doesn't have free spots on defense, either.</p><p>Blue Jackets forward Dmitri Voronkov is another Russian struggling to crack his team's lineup this season, pushing him into trade rumors. The 26-year-old is huge (6-5 and 230 pounds) and has scored 40 goals over the last two NHL seasons combined.</p><p>He might just be a poor man's version of Tyler Bertuzzi, though, and his skating and work ethic don't get rave reviews. He'll be a restricted free agent after his summer.</p><p>Canucks forward Jake DeBrusk, meanwhile, is a more established Bertuzzi-like player who has been taking shots and scoring on a decent percentage of them around the net for years — even though he, like Bertuzzi, tends to be streaky.</p><p>He's a decent skater, too. But he's 30 years old (although he hasn't shown signs of decline yet) and wields a full no-movement clause, which has prevented the rebuilding Canucks from trading him up to this point. He still has four years left on his contract.</p><p>The most ideal target might be Flyers forward Owen Tippett, but it's far from certain the Flyers are willing to trade him — with good reason, because he's a quality player.</p><p>Tippett, 27, is a great skater with good size (6-1 and 210 pounds) and a fire-away shooting mentality that would fit perfectly on the Hawks. He has recorded between 43 and 53 points in four consecutive seasons to go along with excellent analytics. He has six contract years left with a reasonable $6.2 million salary-cap hit.</p><p>He's only worth mentioning because the Hawks and Flyers are both off to terrible starts after entering the season with real ambitions. They could shake up each other's struggling rosters with one move.</p><p>It's unclear, too, if Davidson would be willing to part with any of his young roster players. He would likely be more eager to trade some of his three first-round and two second-round picks in the 2027 draft.</p>
